SECTION 1: Welcome & Introduction
Welcome to the Department of Physics and the McWilliams Center for Cosmology and
Astrophysics in the Mellon College of Science (MCS) at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU)! Our
vibrant research community brings together faculty, postdoctoral scholars, and students
conducting research ranging from stars and black holes to galaxies and the universe.
The Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. program prepares graduate students to be at the
forefront of astronomical discovery, computational astrophysics, data science, and artificial
intelligence. Through rigorous coursework, research, and professional development, students
acquire the knowledge, skills, and experience needed for successful careers in academia,
industry, government, and other research-intensive fields.
This handbook provides an overview of the academic requirements, research expectations,
program policies, and resources for the Ph.D. program. We encourage you to read this
handbook carefully at the beginning of the program and refer to it throughout your graduate
studies. While this handbook is specific to your academic experience in the Department, it is
just one element of the Graduate Student Handbook Suite. There are several other resources
within the suite that you should consult when needed:
●​ The Physics Doctoral Student Handbook contains sections that may be relevant to all
doctoral students in the Department.
●​ The University-wide Graduate Student Handbook outlines critical processes and
policies for all graduate students at Carnegie Mellon.
●​ The Carnegie Mellon Student Handbook contains information and resources to help
you create your Carnegie Mellon experience and embrace your role as a valued
member of our university.
SECTION 2: Program Vision, Mission, and Values
2.1: Vision
To be leaders in the quest to advance humanity’s understanding of the physical world and a
nexus for science at CMU.
2.2: Mission
To achieve this Vision, we will
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 3
●​ Enhance our areas of research strength while thinking boldly in order to seize new
opportunities.
●​ Combine the unique contributions of Physics with the strengths of CMU.
●​ Educate and mentor future generations to succeed in a wide spectrum of careers.
Increase appreciation of the contribution that Physics makes to CMU, the wider community,
and the world at large.
2.3: Values
As a dynamic and collegial community, we value:
●​ Blue sky thinking, collaboration, excellence, and agility.
●​ Diversity.
●​ Fostering the talents of all our members and supporting their ambitions.
Gaining a deeper knowledge of our world—both for the sake of pure understanding and as
the source of technological innovation.
SECTION 3: Degrees Offered
A new graduate program in Astronomy and Astrophysics was approved by the Department of
Physics and the Mellon College of Science in 2025 and will welcome its first cohort in the
2026–2027 academic year. Upon successful completion of the program requirements,
students will be awarded the degree of Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) in Astronomy and
Astrophysics, as it appears on the official diploma.
The Department also offers a Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) in Physics and a Master of Science
(M.S.) in Modern Physics. Information about these degrees is available in their respective
graduate student handbooks.
Immigration changes may impact an F-1 or J-1 student’s ability to change their academic
program, even if allowed to by the program. Students on F-1 or J-1 documents should
proactively consult with the Office of International Education (OIE) when considering a
program change.

SECTION 5: Departmental Resources
The Department Resources Canvas Page maintains a comprehensive and regularly updated
collection of physical and online resources for students. Students are encouraged to review
this page upon arrival at CMU to familiarize themselves with available resources. It also
includes current announcements and opportunities, including courses, workshops, summer
schools, graduate fellowships, postdoctoral positions, and job openings.
Offices and keys are assigned and managed by departmental administrative coordinators.
Students receive keys to their offices and other required spaces, including the graduate
lounge and mailroom. Some rooms, such as department-managed classrooms and meeting
rooms, require keycard access through a CMU ID card. Students who require access should
contact a departmental administrative coordinator, who will add their ID card to the list of
authorized users.
Mailboxes are assigned to students and should be checked regularly. Outgoing mail bins are
available for campus mail, stamped external mail, and external mail requiring departmental
postage. Mailbox assignments are updated annually at the start of the academic year.
Printers and copiers are located in the mailroom and are available for printing, copying, and
scanning. Both black-and-white and color printing are supported. Instructions are available on
the Departmental Resources Canvas Page, and additional support can be obtained from the
MCS Director of Information Technology. Physical copies should be recorded in the logbook,
including the user name or associated course number. Scanned materials can be sent as PDFs
to a designated email address. Users should restock paper as needed, clear minor paper jams
when possible, and notify departmental staff when supplies are low.
Supplies commonly used for office and classroom activities are available in limited quantities
in the mailroom. A detailed inventory list is provided on the Departmental Resources Canvas
Page.
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 6
SECTION 6: Advising
6.1: Role of an Advisor and Advisor Assignments
The Program Director serves as the primary academic advisor for students enrolled in the
Ph.D. program and provides guidance on academic requirements, program policies,
professional development, and other matters related to progress toward the Ph.D. degree.
The Program Director is also available to support students experiencing personal or
professional challenges that may affect their academic success, research progress, or
well-being and can assist in connecting students with appropriate University resources.
In addition, the Director of Graduate Studies oversees graduate education within the
Department and serves as an additional resource for students seeking guidance on
departmental policies, academic matters, or other concerns that may affect their progress
toward the degree. They also carry out TA assignments for all doctoral students regardless of
degree program.
Pre-candidacy students are expected to meet with the Program Director at least once each
semester to review academic progress, discuss upcoming milestones, and address any
questions regarding the Ph.D. program. After advancing to candidacy, students are
encouraged to consult with the Program Director as needed.
Each student is expected to identify a research advisor and join a research group within the
first two weeks of their first semester. The research advisor serves as the student's primary
mentor and provides guidance on research, professional development, and progress toward
the dissertation. Students are expected to meet regularly with their research advisor, typically
on a weekly or biweekly basis through individual meetings, research group meetings, or a
combination of both.
A student who wishes to change research advisors should first discuss the matter with the
current advisor whenever appropriate. The student should then consult with the Program
Director and the Director of Graduate Studies to facilitate a smooth transition and ensure
continuity of academic and research progress. The Department recognizes that advising
relationships may evolve over time and will work with students and faculty to facilitate advisor
changes when necessary.
The Department monitors student progress toward completion of degree requirements. If a
student is determined to be making inadequate progress toward the Ph.D. degree, they will
receive written notification from the Program Director and Department Head. The notification
will identify areas of concern, specify expectations for improvement, and establish a timeline
for addressing deficiencies. Students receiving such notification are encouraged to meet with
their advisor and the Program Director to develop a plan for returning to satisfactory
academic and research progress.
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 7
6.2: Advisor/Advisee Collaboration
The advisor–advisee relationship is a collaborative partnership that plays a central role in a
student’s academic, research, and professional development. Students and advisors are
expected to maintain regular communication and meet on a schedule appropriate to the
student’s stage of study and research activities. These meetings provide opportunities to
discuss research progress, present results, address challenges, establish research goals, and
receive guidance on academic and professional development.
To ensure productive meetings, students should come prepared to discuss their recent
progress, challenges encountered, and plans for future work, along with any relevant
materials. Students are expected to communicate openly, respond to feedback in a timely
manner, and take an active role in managing their academic and research progress. Advisors
are expected to provide constructive feedback, mentorship, and clear expectations regarding
research goals, performance, authorship, and degree milestones.
Students are encouraged to seek guidance from a broad network of mentors, including their
advisor, dissertation committee members, other faculty, postdoctoral fellows, and senior
students. Dissertation committees are typically formed in a student’s second year, and annual
meetings are held with multiple faculty mentors to evaluate progress toward degree
milestones and refine research goals.
Individual Development Plans (IDPs) are meant to promote professional and personal growth
by formally documenting goals and facilitating dialogue, collaboration, and accountability
between advisors and advisees. Carnegie Mellon has developed a set of templates that can be
used by doctoral students and their advisors to create IDPs.
6.3: Review/Redress of Academic Issues
Generally, students should seek informal resolution of academic issues with the relevant
course instructor, research advisor, or other appropriate departmental representative before
initiating formal processes. Students are encouraged to raise concerns directly with the
relevant instructor or advisor, particularly when they involve academic decisions, teaching,
mentoring, or supervision. Faculty are expected to engage in these discussions in good faith
and to view them as part of the normal academic process for clarification and resolution.
If informal discussion does not resolve the issues, students may escalate concerns within the
department by consulting the Program Director, the Director of Graduate Studies, and/or the
Department Head, who can help facilitate further discussion or recommend appropriate next
steps.
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 8
The Department also provides options for submitting anonymous feedback: an anonymous
form for communicating with the Department Head and an anonymous form for
communicating with the Department Climate Community.
Students may also seek guidance from the designated MCS Liaisons for Graduate Affairs for
additional support.
If concerns remain unresolved at the departmental level, students may initiate a formal
review process in accordance with the University’s official appeal and grievance policy.
SECTION 7: Doctoral Degree Requirements
7.1: Residency Requirements
Students enrolled in the Ph.D. program are expected to be in residence at CMU and actively
participate in the academic, research, and other program activities of the Department
throughout their enrollment. Consistent with University policy, Ph.D. students must complete
a minimum of one academic year in residence on a CMU campus. Because the program is
designed for in-person coursework, research mentoring, and professional development,
students are expected to maintain a regular physical presence on campus unless an approved
leave of absence or other formal exception has been granted by the Department and the
University. These residency requirements apply equally to domestic and international
students and are consistent with U.S. immigration regulations governing F-1 and J-1 visa
holders.

Students are strongly encouraged to publish their research as early as possible and regularly
throughout the program. At a minimum, by the end of the Spring semester of their third year,
each student must have either submitted a journal article for publication or formally
submitted a dissertation proposal.
7.3: Registration Process
Students are responsible for registering for courses through the Student Information Online
(SIO).
Prior to registration each semester, students should consult with their research advisor
and/or the Program Director to discuss course selection, research credits, and progress
toward degree requirements. First-year students should meet with the Program Director
before registering to ensure that their course plans align with the Ph.D. curriculum.
7.4: Required Units for Degree Attainment
The Ph.D. program requires the following units for degree attainment:
●​ Three core courses, 12 units each and 36 units total
●​ Three elective courses, 12 units each and 36 units total
●​ Four semesters of the professional development course, 3 units each and 12 units total
●​ First-year research, 60 units total
●​ Dissertation research, 36 units per year
7.5: Core Courses
The Ph.D. program requires completion of three core courses:
●​ 33-731 Stars and Black Holes
●​ 33-732 Galaxies
●​ 33-733 Cosmology
In addition, all pre-candidacy students must enroll in:
●​ 33-735 Professional Development for Astronomy and Astrophysics
7.6: Program Learning Outcomes
The Ph.D. program streamlines learning and training through three core components:
coursework, research, and professional development activities. Students should consult the
course syllabi for detailed learning outcomes. Research skills, including performing literature
reviews, formulating research problems, applying computational and data science methods,
and communicating scientific results, are developed through supervised thesis research.
Students strengthen their scientific writing, oral communication, and critical analysis skills
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 11
through weekly professional development such as seminars, journal clubs, and special topic
sessions.
7.7: Electives
The Ph.D. program requires completion of three elective courses that support the student’s
research and professional goals and are selected in consultation with their research advisor.
They must be approved by the Program Director if not on the pre-approved list below.
Electives may be drawn from physics, statistics, computer science, or other relevant fields.
Approved electives include:
●​ 33-757 Classical Mechanics
●​ 33-788 Special Topics: AI in Particle Physics and Astrophysics
●​ 36-700 Probability and Mathematical Statistics
●​ 10-701 Introduction to Machine Learning
●​ 38-614 Large-Scale Computing in Data Science
●​ 38-615 Computational Modeling, Statistical Analysis, and Machine Learning in Science
7.8: Department Policy on Double Counting Courses
Courses counted toward the Ph.D. in Astronomy and Astrophysics may also be counted
toward the M.S. in Physics. Information on completing an M.S. in Physics while enrolled in the
Ph.D. program is available in the Physics Doctoral Student Handbook.
7.9: Department Policy for Courses Outside the Department/College
Core courses must be completed at CMU. Elective requirements may be fulfilled through
approved graduate-level courses outside the Department or College, subject to approval by
the research advisor and Program Director based on relevance to the student’s academic and
research plan.
Students registered for 36 units may take one course per fall or spring semester at another
Pittsburgh Council on Higher Education (PCHE) institution, subject to approval and availability.
The PCHE is a voluntary consortium of ten accredited colleges and universities in Allegheny
County, Pennsylvania: Carlow University, Carnegie Mellon University, Chatham University,
Community College of Allegheny County, Duquesne University, La Roche University, Pittsburgh
Theological Seminary, Point Park University, Robert Morris University, and the University of
Pittsburgh.
Approved electives at the nearby University of Pittsburgh:
●​ ASTRON3705 Statistics and Data Science
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 12
7.10: Course Exemptions
For the inaugural year of the Ph.D. program, no course exemptions or waivers will be granted
on the basis of prior undergraduate coursework or previously earned graduate degrees. The
program will monitor student progress and solicit feedback and will revisit this policy in
subsequent program reviews.
7.11: Protocol for Evaluation of Transfer Credit
For the inaugural year of the PhD program, no transfer credits will be accepted towards
degree requirements. The program will revisit this policy in subsequent program reviews.
7.12: Teaching Requirements/Opportunities
The Ph.D. program requires each graduate student to serve as a teaching assistant (TA) for at
least one semester before graduation. The teaching requirement is not a condition for
advancement to candidacy but must be completed before the Ph.D. degree is awarded.
TA responsibilities may include leading recitation sections, conducting laboratory sessions,
holding office hours, facilitating student learning, and supporting course instruction.
Assignments consisting solely of grading or staffing a course help center do not satisfy the
teaching requirement. TA and grader appointments may require up to 20 hours of work per
week, although the Department aims to structure most assignments around a typical
workload of approximately 15 hours per week.
Incoming graduate students receive TA training during Department Orientation Week, and
attendance is required for all incoming students. The training focuses on effective
instructional practices, communication skills, classroom management, and strategies for
supporting student learning. Students who complete the training but do not immediately
serve as TAs, such as those supported by fellowships, are encouraged to participate in
refresher training before assuming teaching responsibilities. During the 2026-2027 academic
year, the department is introducing TA training for students beyond their first year, and
doctoral students are expected to comply with the new requirements as they are rolled out.
The Department maintains guidelines outlining the expectations and responsibilities of TAs,
graders, and course instructors on the Department Resources Canvas Page. Additional
teaching-development resources are available through the Eberly Center for Teaching
Excellence and Educational Innovation, which provides workshops, consultations, and
programs to support effective teaching and mentoring.
Graduate students are required to have a certain level of fluency in English before they can
instruct in Pennsylvania, as required by the English Fluency in Higher Education Act of 1990.
Through this Act, all institutions of higher education in the state are required to evaluate and
certify the English fluency of all instructional personnel, including teaching assistants and
interns. The full University policy can be reviewed here.
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 13
The fluency of all instructional personnel will be rated by Language Support in the Student
Academic Success Center to determine at what level of responsibility the student can TA. In
addition to administering the International Teaching Assistant (ITA) Test (a mandatory
screening test for any non-native speaker of English), Language Support in the Student
Academic Success Center helps teaching assistants who are non-native English speakers
develop fluency and cultural understanding to teach successfully at Carnegie Mellon. Visit the
Student Academic Success Center website for additional information.
7.13: Research Requirements/Opportunities
Prior to admission to Ph.D. candidacy, students engage in research training and may enroll in
research-related courses such as 33-775 Introduction to Research I (Fall Year 1), 33-776
Introduction to Research II (Spring Year 1), and 33-997 Graduate Laboratory (Summer Year 1
and thereafter), in consultation with their research advisor and the Program Director.
Following admission to Ph.D. candidacy, students engage in full-time research and typically
enroll in 36 units of 33-998 Thesis Research. The minimum unit load for full-time graduate
student status is 36 units, including a minimum of 24 units in 33-998 Thesis Research.
Research grades are assigned by the research advisor based on progress, engagement, and
satisfactory completion of research activities, in accordance with an established evaluation
rubric. Grades are reported on a letter-grade basis and recorded in accordance with the
University’s Grading Policy.
7.14: Internship/Co-op Requirements and Opportunities
The Ph.D. program does not require internship or co-op experience. Students may pursue
internships or co-op opportunities with approval from their faculty advisor and the Program
Director, provided they are consistent with the student’s academic and research plan.
International students are required to consult with the Office of International Education (OIE)
for eligibility for work authorization before starting or seeking an internship/co-op or
consulting opportunity. International students will benefit from proactively reviewing OIE
guidance regarding off-campus work authorization. Off-campus work authorization
processing times can take several weeks or months, and international students will benefit
from starting the off-campus work authorization process as early as possible.
SECTION 8: Dissertation Preparation &
Requirements
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 14
8.1: PhD Qualifying Exam Requirement
The Ph.D. Qualifying Exam is designed to evaluate a student’s foundational knowledge in
astronomy and astrophysics, understanding of their research area, research progress, and
potential for successful completion of doctoral studies. The examination also assesses the
student’s ability to communicate scientific ideas and respond to questions.
Students are expected to complete the Qualifying Exam in their second year, usually in
January prior to the start of the Spring semester. The Qualifying Exam consists of both written
and oral components.
Written Progress Report: At least two weeks before the examination, the student must
submit a short report describing their research activities and progress. The report should
summarize the scientific background and motivation for the project, objectives, methods,
preliminary results, future research plans, and relevant literature. It should be written in the
style of a journal article and may serve as the foundation for a future publication.
Oral Presentation and Questions: The student will deliver a 30-minute presentation
summarizing the scientific background and motivation for the project, research progress, and
future plans. Following the presentation, the Qualifying Exam Committee will ask questions
addressing the student’s research project and the methods and techniques employed in the
research, as well as broader concepts in astronomy and astrophysics.
The Qualifying Exam Committee will consist of at least three faculty members, who evaluate
the student’s written report, oral presentation, and responses to questions. The student’s
research advisor may attend the examination as a non-voting observer.
Following the examination, the committee will assign a grade of Pass or Fail. Students who do
not pass on the first attempt may retake the exam at the next offering. Failure to pass on the
second attempt will result in dismissal from the Ph.D. program. Students will be notified of the
outcome and any required follow-up actions, typically within the same week.
8.2: PhD Criteria for Advancement to Candidacy
Advancement to Ph.D. candidacy requires:
●​ Successful completion of all three core courses and at least three elective courses, with
a minimum grade of B- in each course.
●​ Successful completion of four semesters of the Professional Development course.
●​ Passing the Qualifying Exam.
Once these requirements are satisfied, the faculty will meet to review the student’s academic
record, performance on the Qualifying Exam, research progress, and overall research
aptitude. Following a positive faculty vote, the student is advanced to Ph.D. candidacy and
begins full-time dissertation research.
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 15
Students are also subject to University requirements governing advancement to candidacy (All
but Dissertation, ABD) status, including applicable timelines, residency expectations, and
tuition and fee structures. Students are responsible for familiarizing themselves with relevant
University Policy for Doctoral Student Status and the ABD Status Agreement Form.
8.3: PhD Dissertation
The Ph.D. dissertation is the culminating scholarly work of the doctoral program and must
demonstrate the student’s ability to conduct independent, original research that makes a
significant contribution to astronomy and astrophysics. The dissertation requirement consists
of at least one research publication, a written dissertation, and a successful public dissertation
defense.
Dissertation Committee: The Dissertation Committee advises the student throughout the
dissertation research and evaluates the written dissertation and final public defense. The
committee is normally proposed by the research advisor in consultation with the student and
consists of at least four members:
●​ the research advisor who serves as Chair
●​ two departmental faculty members with expertise relevant to the dissertation research
●​ one external member from another university or institution with appropriate expertise
The committee should normally be established in time for the student’s first annual
committee meeting following advancement to Ph.D. candidacy. The external committee
member need not be identified before the first annual meeting but must be appointed before
the dissertation defense.
Research Publication or Dissertation Proposal: Students are strongly encouraged to
publish their research as early as possible and regularly throughout the program. At a
minimum, by the end of the Spring semester of their third year, students are expected to
complete either:
●​ a research publication submitted to a peer-reviewed journal
●​ a written dissertation proposal approved by the Dissertation Committee
To facilitate timely progress, students are expected to submit a draft manuscript or proposal
to the Dissertation Committee during the preceding Fall semester. The committee will review
the draft, provide feedback on the scope and progress of the research, and assess whether
the student is on track to complete the dissertation within the expected timeframe. Students
in the Fall semester of their 3rd year who are viewed by their committee as not being on track
to meet this milestone by the end of the Spring semester may be put on academic probation,
with meeting the end of Spring milestone as the necessary condition to get off probation.
Failure to complete the research publication or dissertation proposal by the Spring deadline
may result in dismissal from the Ph.D. program.
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 16
Dissertation: The written dissertation must be submitted to the Dissertation Committee at
least two weeks prior to the defense. It must present the student’s original research and
include a comprehensive description of the motivation, methods, results, and interpretation,
demonstrating mastery of the relevant literature and research techniques.
Defense: The dissertation defense consists of three components:
●​ Public presentation: The candidate presents the dissertation research in an
approximately one-hour talk, followed by questions from the audience.
●​ Closed examination: The Dissertation Committee meets with the candidate in a
closed session to ask further questions and to evaluate the dissertation.
●​ Committee deliberation: The committee meets privately to determine whether the
student has satisfied the requirements for the Ph.D.
The committee may approve the dissertation as submitted, require revisions before granting
final approval, or determine that the dissertation does not satisfy the requirements for the
degree. The committee’s decision and any required revisions are communicated to the
student immediately after the deliberation.
Submission and Certification: Following final approval, the student must submit the
completed dissertation in accordance with University requirements, including formatting,
electronic submission, and any required library or institutional certifications. The University
retains the final approved dissertation in accordance with its dissertation submission and
archival policies.
SECTION 9: Department Policies & Protocols
9.1: Petition Procedures
Students may petition for program-related exceptions or modifications, including program
changes or transfers, course substitutions, and other deviations from standard requirements.
All petitions should clearly state the request and provide appropriate justification. Students
are encouraged to first discuss the matter with their research advisor and the Program
Director. If needed, further consultation may involve the Director of Graduate Studies and the
Department Head.
9.2: Department Policy for Withdrawing from a Course
Students who are considering withdrawing from a course should first discuss the decision
with the course instructor, their research advisor, and the Program Director to understand the
academic implications. Withdrawing from a course may affect progress toward degree
requirements, academic standing, and visa status for international students. The Program
Director can provide guidance on these implications and help students develop an
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 17
appropriate plan of study. Course withdrawals are governed by the University’s Course
Changes Policy and Academic Calendar. Students are responsible for submitting any required
withdrawal requests by the applicable deadlines.
9.3: Requirements for Those Without a Bachelor’s Degree in
Discipline
Students admitted to the Ph.D. program without a prior degree in astronomy and
astrophysics are not required to complete any additional courses, qualifying examinations, or
preparatory requirements beyond those specified in the standard Ph.D. curriculum. All
students follow the same core coursework, research, and degree milestones outlined for the
program.
9.4: Process for Completing a Master’s Degree en route to a PhD
Students may be eligible to receive a Masters of Science (M.S.) in Physics degree en route to
the Ph.D. There is currently no M.S. in Astronomy and Astrophysics degree. The program will
revisit this policy in subsequent program reviews. Information on completing an M.S. in
Physics is available in the Physics Doctoral Student Handbook. Students should consult with
their research advisor and the Program Director to determine their eligibility. International
students should also consult with the Office of International Education (OIE), as immigration
regulations may affect these options.
9.5: New Policies / “Grandfather” Policy
Departmental and College policies, degree requirements, and program procedures may be
revised periodically. In general, students are expected to satisfy the requirements in effect
when they enter the Ph.D. program. However, with the approval of their research advisor and
the Program Director, students may elect to follow subsequent policy changes that are
beneficial to their academic progress. The Program Director will work with students to ensure
a smooth transition when policy changes affect degree requirements or program procedures.
9.6: Time Away from Academic Responsibilities
Students should follow University expectations and consult the Holidays and Time Off
Calendar regarding time away from academic responsibilities. Outside of these holidays, there
is no expectation that time away from academic responsibilities automatically follows the
academic calendar of courses.
Students are expected to coordinate time away from research and other academic duties with
their research advisor. In general, graduate students are expected to continue research
activities during academic breaks and other non-holiday periods, unless alternative
arrangements are made in consultation with their advisor. If students have challenges taking
time off during University holidays due to research continuity or other constraints, they
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 18
should consult with their advisor to arrange for equivalent time off at another time.
9.7: Other Policies and Protocols / Inclusion of Any Variations to
University Policies and Protocols
The Ph.D. program follows all University, College, and Department policies and protocols
without deviation.
SECTION 10: Grading & Evaluation
10.1: Grading Scale/System
The Department follows the University’s Grading Policy, which governs the assignment and
change of grades (including final and mid-semester grades, incompletes, and conditional
failures), grading options (audit and pass/fail), course drops and withdrawals, course repeats,
and grading standards.
All grades are assigned in accordance with the University’s grading scale and are recorded on
the student’s academic transcript: A+ (4.33), A (4.00), A− (3.67), B+ (3.33), B (3.00), B− (2.67), C+
(2.33), C (2.00), C− (1.67), D+ (1.33), D (1.00), and R (0.00).
10.2: Department Policy on Grades for Retaking a Course
Students must earn a passing grade of B− or higher in all three core courses and at least three
elective courses. A student who receives a non-passing grade of C+ or lower in a core course
may retake it only once, at the next offering. A student who receives a non-passing grade in an
elective may retake the same elective or complete another approved elective. Students must
also successfully complete four semesters of the Professional Development course. A student
who receives a non-passing grade in this course must continue to enroll until they satisfy this
program requirement.
10.3: Department Policy on Pass/Fail, Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory
Core and elective courses must be completed for a letter grade and may not be taken on a
pass/fail basis. The Professional Development course and Qualifying Exam are the only Ph.D.
candidacy requirements evaluated as pass/fail.
10.4: Department Policy for Incompletes
The Department follows the University’s Grading Policy for assigning incomplete grades. A
grade of I (Incomplete) may be assigned when a student, for reasons beyond their control, is
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 19
unable to complete course requirements during the academic semester, provided that the
work completed to date is of passing quality and the incomplete does not provide an undue
advantage over other students. The instructor must specify the requirements for completing
the course and designate a default letter grade if the remaining work is not completed.
Students must complete the required coursework no later than the end of the following
academic semester, or sooner if specified by prior agreement.
10.5: Independent Study/Directed Research
Independent study/directed research is not a required or available component of the Ph.D.
program. Students complete research activities through their dissertation research under the
supervision of their research advisor and dissertation committee.
10.6: GPA Requirements and QPA Requirements for Graduation
Students must complete all three core courses and at least three elective courses with a
minimum grade of B− (2.67) in each course. Pre-candidacy students must also complete four
semesters of the Professional Development course. There are no additional GPA or QPA
requirements for graduation beyond the successful completion of all required coursework.
10.7: Satisfactory Academic Standing
Maintaining satisfactory academic standing is a requirement for continued enrollment in the
program. Students who fail to meet this requirement may be placed on academic probation.
Common reasons for probation include, but are not limited to:
●​ A semester GPA below 3.0.
●​ A research grade below B−.
●​ Failure of the Qualifying Exam.
●​ Failure to submit a draft of the required research publication or dissertation proposal
by the end of the Fall semester of the third year.
●​ Failure to complete the required annual research reviews within the expected time
frame.
When placed on academic probation, the student will meet with the Program Director to
review the circumstances leading to probation and develop a plan for returning to good
academic standing. Following this meeting, the Department Head will issue a formal letter
outlining the reasons for probation, the conditions for returning to good standing, and a
realistic timeline for meeting those conditions.
Upon satisfying the conditions outlined in the probation letter within the specified time frame,
the student will be removed from academic probation and receive written confirmation of
their return to good academic standing.
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 20
If the student does not satisfy the conditions within the specified time frame, the student’s
progress will be reviewed by the faculty in a closed meeting. Following this review, the faculty
will determine whether the student may continue in the program. If permitted to continue,
the student will remain on academic probation and receive an updated letter outlining revised
conditions and a timeline for returning to good academic standing. If the faculty determines
that the student may not continue, the student will be dismissed from the program. In such
cases, a short transition period may be granted to allow the student to make appropriate
arrangements for the next steps in their academic or professional career.
Students may appeal decisions regarding academic probation or dismissal in accordance with
the Summary of Graduate Student Appeal and Grievance Procedures.
10.8: Regular Reviews and Evaluations by Department
The Department conducts regular reviews of student progress to ensure satisfactory progress
toward the Ph.D. degree. These reviews include the faculty review for advancement to Ph.D.
candidacy and the annual research reviews conducted by the dissertation committee.
The faculty review for advancement to Ph.D. candidacy evaluates the student’s completion of
required coursework, fulfillment of program requirements, performance on the Qualifying
Exam, and readiness for independent dissertation research. Students who successfully
complete this review advance to Ph.D. candidacy.
Annual research reviews evaluate the student’s progress toward dissertation completion,
including research accomplishments, completion of the required research publication or
dissertation proposal, and plans for future work. Students receive feedback following each
review, including areas requiring improvement and expectations for continued progress.
SECTION 11: Funding & Financial Support
11.1: Statement of Department Financial Support
The Physics Department provides substantial financial support for doctoral students
throughout their Ph.D. program: stipend, tuition, student fees, and Student Healthcare
Insurance Program (SHIP). Students must make satisfactory academic progress and fulfill the
requested teaching or research associated with a funded TA or RA position to be eligible for
financial support.
11.2: Stipend
Doctoral students supported by the department or from a faculty member’s external funding
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 21
receive a stipend for 12 months throughout the year, payable on the 15th and the last
working day of each month. All doctoral students supported by the department (i.e., students
not holding external fellowships) receive the same stipend, regardless of the year entering the
program, teaching responsibilities, or laboratory assignment (see also Sec. 11.13). The
department does not equalize differences in tax withholding. Please note that the first
paycheck arrives on August 31; thus, each incoming student should bring enough money to
pay for any deposits or incidental costs.
The amount of the annual stipend is decided at the college level.
11.3: Tuition
Doctoral students also receive complete tuition remission for the fall and spring semesters.
18 equal tuition payments will automatically post to students’ accounts throughout the
academic year. Students who are not taking courses in the summer are not charged tuition in
the summer. Payment of tuition for any summer classes, including those audited, is the
responsibility of the student.
Additional tuition information is available on the Office of Enrollment Management website.
11.4: Health Insurance Requirements
All full-time students who are physically located in the U.S. are required to meet CMU’s health
insurance policy each academic year. To fulfill this requirement, students must have insurance
that meets university requirements for the duration of their time as an enrolled student,
either through enrolling in the Student Health Insurance Plan (SHIP), or obtaining a SHIP
waiver (for instance because they are still on their parents’ insurance). More details can be
found on Carnegie Mellon’s policy webpage specifying the Medical Insurance Mandate.
Carnegie Mellon covers 100% of the individual premium cost for medical coverage through
the Student Healthcare Insurance Program (SHIP). Doctoral students who have not waived
SHIP by August 15 will see a credit of 100% of the insurance plan fee applied to their student
account by the end of August. Be aware that this applies only to the individual premium for
medical coverage; vision and dental benefits are excluded, but students can also obtain
coverage for those through SHIP (at the students’ own expense). Furthermore, while the 100%
individual premium support only applies to doctoral students, their family members can still
enroll in the university health plan as long as they are prepared to pay the SHIP costs for those
family members.
Students should be aware that the health insurance credit is a non-qualified scholarship, and it
is considered taxable income by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) to all students who receive it.
For international students, the university has an IRS reporting and tax withholding obligation
on non-qualified scholarship payments for students who are considered non-resident aliens
for tax purposes. If you do not qualify for tax treaty benefits, a 14% tax will be withheld from
your health insurance support credit and remitted to the IRS. In this scenario you will see the
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 22
full Ph.D. Insurance Support credited to your student account along with an IRS Tax
Withholding charge equal to 14% of the support. This 14% of the SHIP cost will therefore
appear as a financial obligation (account fee) for the student to pay.
CMU offers a monthly payment option, via Nelnet ($40 enrollment fee each semester), that
allows a student to create a payment plan for their account fees. This option is available at the
beginning of each semester.
For general questions regarding SHIP, please reference the HUB’s Student Account-Related
Health Insurance FAQs.
11.5: Department Fees
Carnegie Mellon charges some additional fees (notably Technology, Student Activities, and
Transportation), as outlined in the University-Wide Graduate Student Handbook, accessible
via the resources webpage maintained by the Office of Graduate and Postdoctoral Affairs. The
Department of Physics does not charge any specific fees in addition to those.
Departmentally supported students are responsible for all other charges not covered by the
department. These include, but are not limited to, federal withhold tax (applied to SHIP),
library fines, optional insurance coverage, summer housing, and other miscellaneous charges.
11.6: Travel/Conference and Research Funding

per student. The year is divided into four (overlapping) half-year periods, with

to each of them. Awards are announced approximately three weeks after each
application deadline. Priority is given to students who present their work at the chosen

●​ Besides conference funding, the Office of Graduate and Postdoctoral Affairs also offers

●​ The Office of Graduate and Postdoctoral Affairs also offers Scholarly Project Funding
(formerly called “GuSH Research Grants”). Small awards of $750, intended to further a

●​ Many funding agencies and scientific societies have specialized conference, research,

11.9: Availability of Summer Employment
If summer support is provided, then students are expected to adhere to the policy for outside
employment described in Sec. 11.10. If summer support is not available, the student may seek
outside employment in consultation with their thesis advisor and the DGS. International
students who wish to explore this option should consult with CMU’s Office of International
Education (OIE) to learn how it may impact their visa status prior to accepting any outside
employment. This policy does not apply to departmentally approved internships.
11.10: Department Policy on Outside Employment
Since students are expected to be enrolled in the doctoral program as full-time students,
seeking outside employment is strongly discouraged. Any students who wish to explore the
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 24
possibility of outside employment must consult with their advisor, the DGS, and the DH in
advance to make sure it does not impact their academic and research progress and fulfillment
of any other obligations associated with their source of funding support (e.g., a TA role). In
addition, international students should consult with CMU’s Office of International Education
(OIE) to learn how outside employment may impact their visa status. This consultation should
occur prior to accepting outside employment.
11.11: Requirements for the Continuation of Funding
Service as a course assistant (TA or grader) is a serious responsibility that impacts the
educational experience of other students in the department. Students with a course assistant
position must demonstrate professionalism and a commitment to this responsibility in order
to remain eligible to hold funded course assistant positions in future. (It is understood that
students may sometimes experience unpredictable personal or academic issues that could
impact their ability to fulfill course assistant responsibilities. As long as they coordinate with
the course instructor to mitigate the impacts of these issues, their eligibility for future
positions will not be affected.) Instructors should convey concerns about TA/grader
performance as outlined in Sec 7.14.
If these concerns are conveyed with at least 4 weeks before final grades are due and are
deemed to be of sufficient severity and/or persistence, the DGS and Department Head may at
their discretion make future course assistant positions for this student contingent on
demonstrated improvement during this semester. This must be conveyed verbally to the
student and in writing to the student and their research advisor. If concerns are conveyed
closer to the end of the semester, the student may have insufficient time to demonstrate an
improvement, but the DGS and Department Head will record the situation and impose
appropriate consequences if the issues recur in subsequent semesters.
11.12: Procedure for Written Notification of Change in Financial
Support
Every effort is made to provide continuous support to students in good standing, within the
limits of the available resources. The Department places a high priority on maintaining
continuous financial support for graduate students and provides notice to students on
changes in their financial support, with a 3-month written notification, where possible, in the
event of a change in the funding. If a student’s funding is lost or reduced unexpectedly and
continuous funding proves difficult to arrange, the student should first consult the DH.
If a student is terminated from the Ph.D. Program, the student’s first notice of a possible
change in financial support will normally be when they are initially placed on probation. The
probationary period will typically last 3–4 months. If conditions for reestablishing good
standing are not met within that time, a student may, depending on departmental resources
and available positions, receive a terminal semester in the department with funding through a
TA position during the academic year or other employment during the summer.
Astronomy and Astrophysics Ph.D. Handbook AY26-27 25
11.13: Department Policy in Graduate Student Equitable Support
As part of the admissions process, any student receiving external financial support for their
PhD program via a scholarship, fellowship, or other means will need to disclose such support
with sufficient details to allow the Physics Department to understand the financial impact.
This includes details regarding the following:
●​ Type of support: Graduate fellowships versus research fellowships
●​ Annual level of student stipend, tuition, student fees, and SHIP support
●​ Duration of external support
Disclosing this information will help the department to understand whether three common
issues will apply to the student for the duration of their external support: (1) inequity in
stipend support, (2) incomplete coverage of other costs (tuition, etc.), (3) any support
restrictions. These situations and other issues related to external fellowships are described
below.
Stipend inequity occurs when the external fellowship support provides a stipend below the
one determined by Mellon College of Science (MCS), which applies to all department
supported PhD students. This situation may make it challenging for the student to cover their
living expenses. When a student’s externally provided stipend is found to be below the Mellon
College of Science’s stipend level, a formal agreement will be made between the department
and student outlining the additional level of support the student may be offered, and the
conditions under which additional support is provided.
The externally supported student’s advisor and the Physics department will agree on how the
additional support is covered for the entirety of the student Ph.D. program. The advisor is
expected to make reasonable attempts to cover that additional support through grant funding
where possible.
A student receiving external support will provide CMU reasonable notification, in advance,
when the terms of that support change.
